title: A bar of 'number of reactions per case' asks how large each surrogate-model problem is
summary: For every ignition-delay target the sensitivity threshold keeps a different number of reactions. The bar chart counts them: high-temperature cases sit in one band, low-temperature cases in another, and one case can stand out. The count controls how many simulations a quadratic surrogate needs.

media.alt: Bar chart of the number of reactions per case. Case index 1 to 45 on the x axis, number of reactions from 0 to above 30 on the y axis. Blue bars for the high-temperature targets (cases 1 to 30) are tall, red bars for the low-temperature targets (cases 31 to 45) get shorter towards the right.

source.caption: Chapter 3. Number of active parameters used to build the p-PRS for high- and low-temperature targets, methyl butanoate
source.note: Two Chapter 3 bar charts, one per fuel, counting how many reactions were kept as active parameters for each ignition-delay target. HTT means high-temperature targets and LTT low-temperature targets, as in the legend. The caption refers to a response surface built from those parameters. No numbers are quoted in this explainer because the chapter is unpublished draft work.

read_the_figure.question: How many reaction parameters does each target need in its surrogate, and does that depend on the temperature regime?
read_the_figure.axes: x: case index, one integer per target (ignition delay at one condition). y: number of reactions that passed the sensitivity selection for that target. Colour: blue for high-temperature targets (HTT), red for low-temperature targets (LTT).
look_at: The two colours form two contiguous blocks: first all high-temperature cases, then all low-temperature cases. Compare the typical bar height of each block.
Local trends in each block. A slow decline of bars means the later targets (hotter, or at later conditions) are controlled by fewer reactions.
Isolated tall or short bars. One short bar in the n-heptane chart looks different from its neighbours and should be checked against its own sensitivity chart.
The two figures are two fuels. Their y axes have different ranges: the methyl butanoate chart runs higher than the n-heptane chart, which is a statement about mechanism size.
Link back to the sensitivity charts: each bar is the number of bars outside the dashed lines in a chart like that one, for one case.
read_the_figure.proves: That the active set is much smaller than the full reaction list for every target, and that the size of the problem depends on regime. It does not say the sets are the same reactions from case to case.
if_wrong: All bars equal: the threshold is not discriminating and the count is set by a cap, not by sensitivity.
A bar of near zero: the case's sensitivity was uniformly low or the case was not processed.
A very tall bar: that case may need a much larger design and a bigger surrogate than its neighbours.
must_check: The selection rule that produced the count is stated (a threshold, same as in the sensitivity charts).
Case numbering is explained (which condition each index is).
Both charts use the same threshold so counts are comparable across fuels.
The y axis starts at zero (it does).

terms.meaning: A rate parameter allowed to vary because its sensitivity passed the threshold.
A low-order polynomial fitted to simulation results as a function of the active parameters, used as a cheap stand-in for the simulation.
A full quadratic polynomial in m variables has this many coefficients.
The table of sampled parameter values (as polynomial terms) used in the least-squares fit.
High-temperature targets and low-temperature targets, as labelled in the legend.
The number of simulations needed grows quickly with the number of parameters, so every dropped parameter pays off.
One ignition-delay target: a fuel at one temperature, pressure and equivalence ratio.

remember: The count is the problem size m of the surrogate.
Quadratic coefficient count grows like m squared over two.
Blocks of colour mean regimes, not different fuels.
A count says how many, not which.
Fewer active parameters, fewer simulations, but also a risk of dropping something that matters elsewhere.

steps.title: Number of terms in a full quadratic
steps.note: One constant, m linear terms, m squared terms, and m(m-1)/2 cross terms. This is the number of unknowns in the least-squares fit.

steps.title: Fit by least squares
steps.tex: \hat{\mathbf b}=\arg\min_{\mathbf b}\ \lVert \mathbf y-X\mathbf b\rVert^2\ \Rightarrow\ (X^{\top}X)\hat{\mathbf b}=X^{\top}\mathbf y
steps.note: X is the design matrix, y the simulated responses at the sampled parameter sets. The normal equations have a unique solution only if X has full column rank, so at least N_coef well-spread samples are needed.

steps.title: Why more parameters cost so much
steps.note: With oversampling by a factor c to control noise and conditioning, the number of simulations per case is c times N_coef. Halving m cuts the cost roughly by four for large m.

steps.title: Counting from a threshold
steps.note: For case c the bar height is the number of reactions whose first-order sensitivity magnitude is at least theta, as read from a chart like the sensitivity figures in this thesis group.

steps.title: Cost over a set of cases
steps.note: If each case has its own surrogate, the total simulation budget is the sum of the individual sizes. If the active sets overlap, one shared surrogate over their union may be cheaper or costlier, depending on the union size.

worked.title: Surrogate size for three illustrative counts
worked.problem: Using illustrative active-parameter counts of m = 10, 20 and 30 (not read from the figure), how many coefficients does a full quadratic need?
worked.answer: 66, 231 and 496 coefficients. Tripling the number of parameters multiplies the surrogate size by about seven, which is why the thresholding in the sensitivity charts matters.

analyze.q: Why might the low-temperature block of bars decrease towards the right while the high-temperature block fluctuates?
analyze.hint: What changes systematically along the case index?

analyze.q: The n-heptane chart has one very short bar. Give two explanations and say which figure in the group would help decide.
If every case kept the same reactions, what would the bar chart look like?

evaluate.q: Is it better to build one surrogate per case or one shared surrogate for all cases? State the cost and risk of each.
evaluate.hint: Union of active sets, conditioning of the design matrix, transfer between cases.

evaluate.q: What extra evidence would show that dropping reactions below the threshold did not hurt accuracy?
evaluate.hint: Held-out comparison of the surrogate with the full simulation.

create: Redraw the chart as a stacked bar showing the shared core of reactions (active in every case of the block) and the case-specific extras.
Design a plot of surrogate size (quadratic coefficient count) against case index, so the reader sees cost directly instead of parameter count.

checks.answer: For one ignition-delay target, the number of reactions whose sensitivity passed the selection threshold, i.e. how many parameters its surrogate model has.

checks.q: How many coefficients does a full quadratic need for m = 15 active parameters?
Why does the number of simulations grow faster than the number of parameters?
checks.answer: A quadratic has m(m-1)/2 cross terms in addition to the 2m + 1 others, so the coefficient count grows like m squared over two.

checks.q: A bar is half the height of the others. Is that case easier or just different?
checks.hint: A short bar may be a failure of the selection.
checks.answer: Not necessarily easier: it may reflect a low-sensitivity case or a processing error. Check its sensitivity chart before trusting a small surrogate.

checks.q: How would you choose a threshold so that every case gets a similar number of active parameters?
checks.answer: Keep the top-k reactions by absolute sensitivity for each case, with k set by the budget, instead of a fixed value threshold. The counts would be constant, and the cost would be fixed.
